_: Shared behavioural table for the budget refusals and the variance verdict — see scripts/check-mirrors.js check 14. `jayhind-client-back/src/const/budget.const.ts` enforces them; `jayhindi-client-front/src/utils/budget-rules.util.ts` states them on the budget dialog so an operator reads the reason instead of meeting a 400. Both must answer every expanded row with the SAME SENTENCE, and both must match the sentence stated here — so a wording one side quietly improved, and a rule both sides forgot together, are different failures.
__regions: A case's `given` holds ARRAYS: every combination is expanded and compared, so a case is a statement about a REGION of the fact space rather than one row. The line rules are split along the three TARGET KINDS, because the duplicate sentence names the kind and `cost-centre` is rendered as `cost centre` — a table that dodged that would stop comparing the wording that reaches the screen.
__literal: `lineSet` is declared `literal` in check 14: its fact space is a LIST of lines, not a product of scalars, and expanding an array of lines would silently turn one multi-line case into N single-line ones — which is the opposite of what a duplicate-detection vector is about. The same call check 13 makes for `classLines`.
__verdict: The `direction` and `verdict` sections are KEPT as documentation of the rule and are no longer compared by check 14 — see that check's own note. P8b-2 mirrored them into the browser, the copy had no reader (the report renders the verdict the API sends), and the UI gate proved it by injecting a wrong verdict into that copy and passing 6/6. What checks the rendering is qa-artifacts/tests/ui/masters/budget-rules.ts, a third copy compared against what the screen shows. A mirror with no reader is not a mirror.

messages.line-no-target: A budget line has to be set on something — choose an account group, a ledger or a cost centre.
messages.line-many-targets: A budget line is set on exactly one of an account group, a ledger or a cost centre, not several at once — otherwise there is no single figure to compare it against.
messages.line-no-amount: A budget line needs an amount.
messages.line-negative: A budget amount is a target figure, so it cannot be negative — which side of the books it falls on is decided by the head it is set on, not by its sign.
messages.line-bad-basis: "${basis}" is not a budget basis — it is either a closing balance or nett transactions.
messages.budget-half-open: A budget covers a period, so it needs both a start and an end date — there is nothing to compare a target against without them.
messages.budget-backwards: A budget's period cannot end (${periodTo}) before it starts (${periodFrom}).
messages.set-dup-group: This budget already has a line on that group — one target per budget, or there are two answers to what it is.
messages.set-dup-ledger: This budget already has a line on that ledger — one target per budget, or there are two answers to what it is.
messages.set-dup-centre: This budget already has a line on that cost centre — one target per budget, or there are two answers to what it is.

line.why: A well-formed ledger line, and a ZERO amount is deliberately among them: 'budget nothing for entertainment' is a real instruction. An absent basis is fine because the COLUMN carries the default, never the DTO (BUG-0020).
A group target — a whole subtree of the chart of accounts.
A cost-centre target — one part of the business, across every head it spends on.
An explicit `null` is unset, which is what the COLUMNS hold — a rule reading it as 'named' would refuse every line a form submits.
Nothing named. ⚠️ This is checked BEFORE the amount, so an empty new row says what it needs rather than complaining about a figure the operator has not reached yet.
A group AND a ledger — two answers to what the budget is on, and they can disagree.
A group AND a cost centre. The second is not even on a statement, so the pair is not merely redundant.
A ledger AND a cost centre.
All three. One sentence covers every over-named shape, so the count does not leak into the wording.
A target with no figure is not a target.
⚠️ Checked AFTER the target rule, so a line with one target and no amount says which of the two it is missing.
⚠️ The sentence names what DECIDES the side — the head, not the sign — because an operator who typed a minus was reasoning about a credit balance and needs telling that the head already says so.
The same on a group target: the rule is about the amount, not about which kind of head it is on.
⚠️ An empty string is among them: it is not `null`, so it is a stated basis and a wrong one. A rule that treated it as absent would silently store the column default under a value the caller chose.

header.why: A named, bounded period — and a SINGLE-DAY one, because both ends are inclusive.
Whitespace is not a name — both sides trim before deciding, or a screen accepts a budget nobody can find in a picker.

⚠️ Both ends required, UNLIKE a tax slab's validity (D-50) where an absent bound means 'still in force' and is a real state. Here the closing-balance basis needs a last day to stand at and the nett basis a window to move within.
The other half-open shape. One sentence covers both, so the wording does not leak which end is missing.
⚠️ The sentence QUOTES BOTH DAYS, because the operator has two date pickers open and needs to know which one to move.

lineSet.why: ⚠️ Group 5, ledger 5 and centre 5 are three DIFFERENT things. Only the pair (kind, id) identifies a target, and a rule keyed on the id alone would refuse a perfectly ordinary budget.
A budget with no lines yet is a real and common state — it is what every budget is one second after it is created.
Two answers to what that ledger's target is, and every report below would pick whichever the sort produced.
A duplicate that is not adjacent — the rule carries a seen-set rather than comparing neighbours.
⚠️ The sentence renders `cost-centre` as `cost centre`. A table that only covered the other two kinds would stop comparing this wording.
⚠️ Two bases on one head is still TWO, not a richer statement: the report reads one figure per head.

⚠️ A line naming NOTHING is left to the per-line rule rather than double-reported here. Two malformed lines are not 'a duplicate', and a set rule that claimed them would put the wrong sentence under the operator's cursor.
A malformed line does not mask a real duplicate elsewhere in the set.

direction.why: Coming in under an expense budget is the thing a budget is usually for.
Beating a revenue target is good.

⚠️ THE ROW THAT MATTERS. A cash target wants to be exceeded and a debtors target does not, and both are Assets; a borrowing limit wants to be undershot and share capital overshot, and both are Liabilities. A screen that coloured an Asset overshoot red because an Expense overshoot is red would be inventing an opinion about somebody's balance sheet.

⚠️ No nature at all — `Suspense A/c` and `Branch / Divisions` have no side of the books. The lower-case and upper-case spellings are here because the two sides read this value from DIFFERENT places (a TS enum and a JSON string), and a case-insensitive match on one side only is exactly the drift check 14 exists to catch.

verdict.why: No direction means no verdict, whichever way the figure went.

⚠️ A figure that HIT its target is neither favourable nor adverse — and the tolerance matters: both sides round to the paisa first, so 0.004 is nil. Calling nil favourable would make every head budgeted to zero and left alone a success story, which is most heads in most budgets.

__interp: The message templates interpolate the ROW keys, so a backwards period names ${periodFrom}/${periodTo} rather than ${from}/${to}. The sentence the code builds normalises through toIsoDay first, which is identity for the ISO strings this table uses — a Date-valued vector would need the table to state the normalised day.
__oneTarget: ⚠️ Every `line` region names EXACTLY ONE target, and the arrays vary only the other fields. The first cut of this table varied `ledgerId: [7, null]` alongside a null `groupId`, so the cross-product quietly included a row with NO target and another with two — and the `line-negative` region then met the 'exactly one' refusal instead of the negative-amount one. A region has to be a statement about the part of the fact space it claims, or the expansion invents rows the case was never about.

delete.why: ⚠️ It returns `null` unconditionally and exists to SAY SO — `describeClassDeleteBlock`'s shape one phase over. Nothing in the schema points at a `budgets` row: no journal line, no voucher, no allocation, so §4.9 rule 2's 'a record that ever posted archives' has nothing to bite on. If a future phase ever posts from a budget — a provision, say — this is the function that has to grow a reason, and this vector is what will notice both sides growing it differently.
